items.stem: By 1914 the Great Powers of Europe were divided into two armed alliances. Describe the alliance system in Europe by 1914.
items.answer: The Triple Alliance (1882) linked Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy. The Triple Entente linked Britain, France and Russia by 1907. France and Russia had a military alliance from 1894. Alliances meant a dispute between two powers could draw in the others. Britain's ententes were understandings rather than binding military alliances.

items.stem: Consider this view: “The alliance system was the main cause of the First World War.” Give one reason to agree and one reason to disagree.
items.answer: For: Alliances turned a quarrel between Austria-Hungary and Serbia into a war between the Great Powers within a week. Against: Italy ignored the Triple Alliance and Britain's entente was not binding, so alliances did not force everyone to fight. Judgement: Alliances explain why the war spread, but militarism, rigid war plans and Balkan nationalism explain why a crisis became war; the alliances were important but not sufficient on their own.

items.stem: On 11 November 1918 an armistice ended the fighting on the Western Front. (a) Describe how the great empires of Europe were affected by the end of the war. [4] (b) Why did Germany ask for an armistice in 1918? [6]
items.answer: (a) The Russian Empire collapsed in 1917 when the Tsar abdicated and the Bolsheviks took power. The German Empire ended when the Kaiser abdicated in November 1918. Austria-Hungary broke apart in October-November 1918 into Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and other states. The Ottoman Empire was defeated and signed the armistice of Mudros in October 1918. (b) The Ludendorff (Spring) Offensive failed and exhausted the German army. The Allied Hundred Days Offensive from August 1918 pushed the Germans back. Fresh American troops were arriving in large numbers. The British blockade caused hunger and unrest at home, ending in mutiny and revolution. Germany's allies Bulgaria, the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary all made peace in autumn 1918.

items.stem: ‘The arrival of American troops was the main reason why Germany asked for an armistice in 1918.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: By mid-1918 around 10,000 US troops were arriving in France each day, giving the Allies a growing advantage. The prospect of millions more Americans made German victory impossible. Against: The failure of the Ludendorff Offensive cost Germany its best troops. The Allied offensive from Amiens in August 1918 was led mainly by British Empire and French forces. The blockade caused hunger, strikes and mutiny. The collapse of Germany's allies left it isolated. Judgement: US troops mattered mostly by removing hope of victory; military defeat after the failed spring offensive and collapse at home were more immediate causes.

items.stem: On 11 November 1918 an armistice ended the fighting on the Western Front. What were the terms of the armistice of 11 November 1918?
items.answer: German forces had to leave occupied France, Belgium and Alsace-Lorraine. Allied troops would occupy the left bank of the Rhine. Germany handed over large quantities of weapons, including artillery, machine guns and aircraft. Germany surrendered its submarines and its surface fleet was interned. The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk was cancelled and the Allied blockade continued.

items.stem: How important was the collapse of empires in shaping the problems facing the peacemakers in 1919? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Whole regions of central and eastern Europe needed new borders and governments. Mixed populations meant self-determination could not satisfy everyone, leaving minorities in new states. Bolshevik Russia was absent and feared. Against: The victors' own aims (security, revenge, reparations) also caused problems. Public opinion in Britain and France demanded harsh terms for Germany. Wilson's ideals clashed with the secret wartime treaties. Judgement: The collapse of empires created the hardest territorial problems, but the clash between the Big Three's aims was the key problem for the German settlement.

items.stem: In January 1918 President Woodrow Wilson set out the USA's war aims in the Fourteen Points. (a) Describe the main ideas of Wilson's Fourteen Points. [4] (b) Why did Wilson put forward the Fourteen Points? [6]
items.answer: (a) No more secret treaties (open diplomacy). Freedom of the seas for all nations. Free trade and the removal of economic barriers. Reduction of armaments by all countries. Self-determination for the peoples of eastern Europe, including an independent Poland. A general association of nations to keep the peace. (b) He believed the war had been caused by secret alliances and arms races, so wanted open diplomacy and disarmament. He wanted a just peace so that Germany would not seek revenge. He wanted to spread democracy and self-determination. He hoped a League of Nations would prevent future wars. As an American he favoured free trade and freedom of the seas.

items.stem: In January 1918 President Woodrow Wilson set out the USA's war aims in the Fourteen Points. (a) What did Wilson mean by self-determination? [4] (b) Why was self-determination difficult to apply in eastern Europe? [6]
items.answer: (a) National groups should be able to choose their own government. Borders should follow lines of nationality where possible. Peoples of Austria-Hungary should have the chance of autonomous development. Plebiscites (votes) could decide disputed areas. (b) Different national groups were mixed together, so any border left minorities. New states needed defensible borders and resources, which sometimes meant including other peoples. The Allies would not apply it to Germans, for example in Austria and the Sudetenland. Wartime promises to Italy and others conflicted with it.

items.stem: ‘The alliance system was the main cause of the First World War.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer. In your answer you may wish to consider: the Schlieffen Plan; the naval race; the alliances.
items.answer: For: Alliances turned a quarrel between Austria-Hungary and Serbia into a war between the Great Powers within a week. The blank cheque and the Franco-Russian alliance meant each power felt obliged to act. Against: Italy ignored the Triple Alliance and Britain's entente was not binding, so alliances did not force everyone to fight. The naval race and militarism created fear and rigid war plans such as the Schlieffen Plan. Balkan nationalism and the assassination provided the spark. Imperial rivalry in Morocco and elsewhere had already raised tension. Judgement: Alliances explain why the war spread, but militarism, rigid war plans and Balkan nationalism explain why a crisis became war; the alliances were important but not sufficient on their own.

items.stem: Describe the situation in Germany in November 1918.
items.answer: Sailors mutinied at Kiel and revolution spread, with workers' and soldiers' councils set up in many cities. The British naval blockade had caused severe food shortages. Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated on 9 November and fled to the Netherlands. A republic was proclaimed and Friedrich Ebert led a new government. The new government agreed to the armistice on 11 November.

items.stem: Wilson hoped the peace would be based on justice and self-determination rather than revenge. How far was the principle of self-determination applied in the peace settlement of 1919-20? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and the Baltic states were created or recognised. Plebiscites were held in areas such as Schleswig and Upper Silesia. Against: Germans were denied union with Austria and placed in Czechoslovakia and Poland. New states contained large minorities. Former German and Ottoman colonies became mandates of Britain and France rather than independent. Judgement: Self-determination was applied widely in eastern Europe but selectively, and not to Germans or colonial peoples.

items.stem: Why did the assassination of Franz Ferdinand lead to a general European war? Give one reason.
items.answer: Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia, sent a harsh ultimatum and declared war on 28 July 1914.

Russia, as protector of the Slavs, mobilised to support Serbia. Germany had promised to back Austria-Hungary (the “blank cheque”) and declared war on Russia on 1 August and France on 3 August. The Schlieffen Plan sent German troops through neutral Belgium, which brought Britain into the war on 4 August. [1]

items.stem: How far was Germany responsible for the outbreak of war in 1914? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: The blank cheque encouraged Austria-Hungary to attack Serbia. Germany declared war on Russia and France and invaded Belgium, which brought Britain in. Weltpolitik and the naval race raised international tension. Against: Austria-Hungary chose to issue the ultimatum and declare war on Serbia. Russia's general mobilisation made war more likely. Serbian nationalists carried out the assassination; all the powers had arms races and war plans. Judgement: Germany carried a large share of responsibility through the blank cheque and the Schlieffen Plan, but responsibility was shared, especially with Austria-Hungary and Russia.

items.stem: What were the terms of the armistice of 11 November 1918?
items.answer: German forces had to leave occupied France, Belgium and Alsace-Lorraine. Allied troops would occupy the left bank of the Rhine. Germany handed over large quantities of weapons, including artillery, machine guns and aircraft. Germany surrendered its submarines and its surface fleet was interned. The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk was cancelled and the Allied blockade continued.
